title: Switching mid-action
plainEnglish: It says you were doing one action and then, partway through, switched to or were interrupted by another.
whenToUse: Reach for -다가 when you start an action, leave it unfinished, and a second action cuts in or takes over, very often unplanned: 집에 가다가 편의점에 들렀어요 (I was on my way home and stopped by the convenience store). It is the everyday way to narrate the in-between of one action where something else happened. It also covers a setting you were in that changed: 자다가 깼어요 (I was sleeping and woke up). The intent is to flag that the first action was cut short, not completed, so the listener pictures you mid-stride when the next thing occurred.
attachmentRule: Attach -다가 (often shortened to -다) straight to the plain verb stem with no vowel change (가다→가다가, 먹다→먹다가, 보다→보다가). The subject of both clauses must be the same person, and the first action is left unfinished. For a finished action that then leads to a result, you can use the past stem -았/었다가 (갔다가 = went and then came back).
contrastWith: -다가 vs -고 나서: -다가 cuts the first action short to do another (집에 가다가 친구를 만났어요 = on the way, never arriving yet), while -고 나서 finishes it completely first (집에 가고 나서 친구를 만났어요 = got home, then met). -다가 vs -자마자: -자마자 means the first action fully ends and the second instantly follows (집에 오자마자 = the moment I arrived), whereas -다가 keeps the first action still in progress when the switch happens. If the verb is over, it cannot be -다가.

examples.ko: 자다가 깼어요.
examples.en: I was sleeping and woke up.

examples.ko: 드라마를 보다가 잠들었어요.
examples.en: I was watching a drama and fell asleep.

examples.ko: 버스를 타고 가다가 멀미가 나서 중간에 내렸어요.
examples.en: I was riding the bus, got motion sick, and got off partway.

commonMistakes: Using -다가 with two different subjects, like 제가 요리하다가 친구가 왔어요; both actions must be the same person, so for a different doer use a separate clause such as 제가 요리하고 있는데 친구가 왔어요.

Conjugating the verb before -다가, like 먹어다가 or 갔다가 for an unfinished action; attach -다가 to the plain stem (먹다가, 가다가), and reserve -았/었다가 only for an action that fully finished and then reversed (집에 갔다가 다시 나왔어요).

practiceItems.prompt: I was going home and (met a friend)
I was watching a drama and (fell asleep)
I was working and (suddenly got a headache)

studyOrder: Find the first action you start but do not finish
Attach -다가 to its plain stem
Make sure the same person does both actions
Add the new or interrupting action in the second clause
beginnerExplanation: V-다(가) captures that very common moment when you are in the middle of doing something and then switch to, or get interrupted by, something else. Picture a movie freezing mid-scene and cutting away: that pause is -다가. You simply glue -다가 (you will often hear it cut to just -다) onto the plain verb stem, so 가다 becomes 가다가 and 보다 becomes 보다가. Example: 집에 가다가 친구를 만났어요 means I was heading home and ran into a friend along the way, with home never actually reached. Two rules keep it natural: the same person must do both actions, and you attach it to the bare stem, never a conjugated form like 먹어다가. Contrast it with -고 나서, where you completely finish the first action before moving on, whereas -다가 always leaves the first action hanging in mid-air.

title: Because of (sudden, bad) cause
plainEnglish: It gives a sudden or unintended reason that caused an unwanted result.
whenToUse: Use -는 바람에 to pin an unexpected, usually out-of-your-control event as the cause of something that went wrong: 늦잠을 자는 바람에 지하철을 놓쳤어요 (I overslept, so I missed the subway). The intent is mild blame or excuse-making, presenting the cause as something that happened to you rather than a choice you made. It fits accidents, sudden weather, breakdowns, and other people's actions that derailed your plan: 컴퓨터가 갑자기 멈추는 바람에 처음부터 다시 시작했어요. If the outcome is neutral or good, this pattern feels wrong, because 바람에 carries a built-in sense of trouble. The noun 바람 here means a gust or sudden force, so literally the result was blown off course by that cause.
attachmentRule: Attach -는 바람에 to a verb stem (자다→자는 바람에, 막히다→막히는 바람에). It only goes on action verbs, not adjectives, and even though it describes a past result you keep the form as -는 바람에, not a past form. The result clause is almost always negative or unplanned and is normally in the past tense.
contrastWith: -는 바람에 vs -아/어서: 바람에 blames a sudden, unintended, bad cause (비가 오는 바람에 다 젖었어요 = it suddenly rained and I got soaked), while -아/어서 is a neutral all-purpose because that works for any result, good or bad (비가 와서 우산을 샀어요). -는 바람에 vs -느라고: 느라고 blames YOUR own time-consuming action that you were busy with (게임하느라고 못 잤어요), whereas 바람에 usually blames an external event that hit you, and unlike 느라고 it does not require the same subject.

examples.ko: 갑자기 비가 오는 바람에 다 젖었어요.
examples.en: It suddenly rained, so I got completely soaked.

examples.ko: 길이 막히는 바람에 약속에 삼십 분이나 늦었어요.
examples.en: The traffic was jammed, so I was a whole thirty minutes late to my appointment.

examples.ko: 옆 사람이 미는 바람에 들고 있던 커피를 쏟았어요.
examples.en: The person next to me shoved me, so I spilled the coffee I was holding.

commonMistakes: Attaching it to an adjective, like 바빠서 갈 수 없는데 바쁜 바람에; it goes only on action verbs, so for a state-based excuse use -아/어서 (바빠서 못 갔어요) instead.

Putting it on a past stem, like 잤는 바람에 or 왔는 바람에; keep the present shape -는 바람에 even when the result already happened, because the form stays fixed and only the final verb shows past tense (자는 바람에 늦었어요).

practiceItems.prompt: I overslept, so (I was late to work)
the traffic was jammed, so (I was late)
it suddenly rained, so (I got soaked)
practiceItems.ko: 갑자기 비가 오는 바람에 다 젖었어요.
practiceItems.answer: 갑자기 비가 오는 바람에 다 젖었어요.

studyOrder: Find the sudden action or event that caused trouble
Attach -는 바람에 to its verb stem
Keep it in the -는 form even for a past result
State the negative or unplanned result in the past tense
beginnerExplanation: V-는 바람에 is the connector you reach for when something unexpected goes wrong and you want to pin the blame on its cause. The noun 바람 literally means a gust of wind, so imagine your plans getting knocked off course by a sudden blast — that image is the whole feeling of this pattern. You add -는 바람에 to an action verb stem, so 자다 becomes 자는 바람에 and 막히다 becomes 막히는 바람에. The result is always a sudden, usually unwanted cause leading to a bad outcome, as in 늦잠을 자는 바람에 지각했어요 (I overslept, so I was late). Two things trip learners up: it only attaches to action verbs, not adjectives, so 바쁜 바람에 is wrong; and even though the result already happened, you keep the present shape 자는 바람에, not 잤는 바람에. Think of it as a more dramatic, blame-assigning cousin of the plain because connector 아/어서.

title: I noticed X, then Y
plainEnglish: It links something you personally observed earlier to a result or change that followed.
whenToUse: Use -더니 to report that you watched someone do or be something over a stretch of time, and then a related, often unsurprising outcome appeared: 동생이 매일 야식을 먹더니 살이 쪘어요 (My brother kept eating late-night snacks, and sure enough he gained weight). The intent is to share a firsthand observation with a sense of cause-and-effect or of I-saw-this-coming. It is also the natural way to mark a contrast over time that you witnessed: 아까는 춥더니 지금은 따뜻해요 (it was cold earlier, but now it's warm). The -더- inside it is the retrospective marker meaning I recall directly perceiving this, which is why it feels personal and eyewitness-like.
attachmentRule: Attach -더니 to the plain stem of a verb or adjective with no vowel change (먹다→먹더니, 춥다→춥더니). For the typical use, the first clause is something you observed about another person or the weather, and the second clause is its natural result. With your own actions, the related form -았/었더니 (먹었더니) is used to mean after I did X, then Y happened.
contrastWith: -더니 vs -아/어서: -더니 reports a result you personally watched unfold after someone else's behavior, carrying eyewitness flavor (친구가 열심히 배우더니 잘해요 = I saw her study hard, and now she's good), while -아/어서 just states a neutral cause with no sense of observation (친구가 열심히 배워서 잘해요). -더니 vs -았/었더니: plain -더니 is for what you observed about OTHERS (동생이 먹더니 살이 쪘어요), whereas -았/었더니 is for YOUR own completed action and its follow-up (제가 운동했더니 다리가 아파요); mixing up the two is the classic slip.

examples.ko: 하늘이 흐리더니 비가 오기 시작했어요.
examples.en: The sky got cloudy, and then it started to rain.

examples.ko: 아까는 날씨가 춥더니 지금은 오히려 더워요.
examples.en: The weather was cold earlier, but now it is actually hot instead.

examples.ko: 동생이 매일 게임만 하더니 결국 시험을 망쳤어요.
examples.en: My brother did nothing but game every day, and in the end he bombed the exam.

commonMistakes: Using plain -더니 about your own action and its result, like 제가 많이 먹더니 배가 아파요; for your own completed action switch to -았/었더니, so 많이 먹었더니 배가 아파요 (I ate a lot, and now my stomach hurts).
Adding vowel harmony before -더니, like 먹어더니 or 추워더니; attach it straight to the plain stem, so 먹더니 and 춥더니, with no -아/어 in between.

practiceItems.prompt: he only gamed every day, and then (he bombed the exam)
it was cold earlier, but now (it is warm)
the sky got cloudy, and then (it started to rain)

studyOrder: Recall something you personally observed earlier
Attach -더니 to that verb or adjective stem
Make the second clause the result or change that followed
For your own actions, switch to -았/었더니 instead
beginnerExplanation: V/A-더니 is how Korean ties together something you watched happen and the result or change that came after it, with a built-in sense of I saw this myself. Think of the -더- inside it as a tiny eyewitness stamp: I was there, I noticed it. You attach -더니 to the plain stem, so 먹다 becomes 먹더니 and 춥다 becomes 춥더니. It shines when describing other people or the weather: 동생이 매일 야식을 먹더니 살이 쪘어요 means my brother kept eating late-night snacks, and sure enough he gained weight. It can also mark a contrast over time, as in 아까는 춥더니 지금은 따뜻해요 (it was cold earlier, but now it is warm). The catch for beginners is the person: -더니 fits things you observed about others, while for your own actions you switch to -았/었더니, as in 운동했더니 다리가 아파요 (I worked out, and now my legs hurt).

title: Since I noticed, so I…
plainEnglish: It gives the reason you noticed that made you spontaneously do something yourself.
whenToUse: Use -길래 when something you saw, heard, or were told prompted you to act on the spot, of your own accord: 딸기가 싸길래 좀 샀어요 (The strawberries were cheap, so I bought some). The intent is to explain your spontaneous reaction by pointing at the trigger you perceived. It is warm and conversational, common in casual speech and storytelling, and it loves reported triggers: 친구가 맛있다고 하길래 저도 시켰어요. Because the reason is something you noticed externally, the second clause is naturally your own past action — your in-the-moment response to that observation. It is the spoken cousin of the slightly more bookish -기에.
attachmentRule: Attach -길래 to the plain stem of a verb or adjective with no vowel change (싸다→싸길래, 울다→울길래, 먹다→먹길래). The first clause is the reason you perceived, and the second clause must be your own action and is usually in the past. For a noun reason use N(이)길래.
contrastWith: -길래 vs -으니까: -길래 is spoken and reaction-based — an external trigger you noticed leads to YOUR own spontaneous action, and it cannot end in a command (딸기가 싸길래 샀어요, never 싸길래 사세요). -으니까 is broader: it can justify commands and suggestions (피곤하니까 쉬세요 = since you're tired, rest) and is fine with any subject. So if you want to tell someone else what to do, you must use -으니까, not -길래.

examples.ko: 날씨가 좋길래 산책하러 나왔어요.
examples.en: The weather was nice, so I came out for a walk.

examples.ko: 아이가 울길래 얼른 안아 줬어요.
examples.en: The child was crying, so I quickly picked her up.

examples.ko: 친구가 그 식당이 맛있다고 하길래 저도 한번 가 봤어요.
examples.en: My friend said that restaurant was good, so I went and tried it too.

commonMistakes: Using a command or suggestion in the second clause, like 싸길래 사세요; the result must be your OWN action you already took, not an order to someone else — for that, switch to -으니까 (싸니까 사세요).

Putting your own planned decision as the reason, like 제가 가기로 했길래; the first clause should be something you perceived from outside (날씨가 좋길래), not your own intention, which would make the trigger-reaction logic collapse.

practiceItems.prompt: the strawberries were cheap, so (I bought two packs)
the child was crying, so (I picked her up)
the weather was nice, so (I came out for a walk)

studyOrder: Find what you saw or heard that prompted you
Attach -길래 to that verb or adjective stem
Make the second clause your own reaction
Usually put your reaction in the past tense
beginnerExplanation: V/A-길래 is a friendly, spoken connector that explains the reason you noticed which pushed you to do something yourself, on the spot. Picture it as I saw an opportunity, so I grabbed it. You add -길래 straight to the stem, so 싸다 becomes 싸길래 and 울다 becomes 울길래. The classic shape is observation then my reaction: 딸기가 싸길래 좀 샀어요 means the strawberries looked cheap, so I went ahead and bought some. The key restriction is that the second clause has to be your own action, very often in the past tense, so you cannot end with a command like 사세요. Think of it as warmer and more conversational than 으니까, and remember the dividing line: 으니까 can justify suggestions and orders, while 길래 only explains what made you, the speaker, act.

title: The more, the more
plainEnglish: It says as one thing increases, another thing changes along with it.
whenToUse: Use -(으)ㄹ수록 for sliding-scale relationships where more of one thing brings more (or less) of another: 한국어는 공부할수록 재미있어요 (The more I study Korean, the more fun it gets). The intent is to show that two things move together by degree, not just that one caused the other once. It is extremely common in opinions, advice, and observations about gradual change: 나이가 들수록 시간이 빨리 가요. Koreans habitually stack -(으)면 in front of the same verb for emphasis — 보면 볼수록, 들으면 들을수록 — which feels even more vivid. Adding 더 (more) or 점점 (gradually) in the result clause sharpens the rising effect.
attachmentRule: Add -을수록 to a stem ending in a consonant (먹다→먹을수록, 작다→작을수록) and -ㄹ수록 to a stem ending in a vowel (가다→갈수록, 크다→클수록). ㄹ-stems drop their ㄹ and take -ㄹ수록 (살다→살수록, 멀다→멀수록). It is very often paired with -(으)면 in front for emphasis, as in 보면 볼수록.
contrastWith: -(으)ㄹ수록 vs -(으)니까: -(으)ㄹ수록 expresses a proportional, sliding scale where both sides rise or change together (사람이 많을수록 시끄러워요 = the more people, the louder), while -(으)니까 just states a one-time cause and effect with no increasing-together feeling (사람이 많으니까 시끄러워요 = since there are many people, it's loud). -(으)ㄹ수록 vs -다가: -다가 marks a switch from one action to another, not a graded change, so they are not interchangeable.

examples.ko: 사람이 많을수록 더 시끄러워요.
examples.en: The more people there are, the louder it gets.

examples.ko: 이 노래는 들을수록 더 좋아져요.
examples.en: The more I listen to this song, the more I come to like it.

examples.ko: 이 책은 읽으면 읽을수록 점점 더 어려워져요.
examples.en: The more I read this book, the harder and harder it gets.

commonMistakes: Using -을수록 after a vowel stem, like 갈을수록 or 클을수록; vowel stems take -ㄹ수록, so 갈수록 and 클수록, and remember ㄹ-stems also use -ㄹ수록 after dropping their ㄹ (살수록).
Spacing it wrong as -ㄹ 수록, like 할 수록; write 수록 attached as one unit (할수록), unlike the separate noun 수록 you might guess from spacing.

practiceItems.prompt: the more I study Korean, (the more fun it gets)
the more I listen to this song, (the more I like it)
the more people there are, (the louder it gets)

studyOrder: Find the thing that increases
Add -을수록 after a consonant or -ㄹ수록 after a vowel
Optionally add -(으)면 in front for emphasis
Put the matching change in the second clause, often with 더
beginnerExplanation: V/A-(으)ㄹ수록 is the Korean version of the more, the more, describing how two things rise or change together on a sliding scale — picture a dial where turning one knob moves the other. The attachment follows the usual sound split: consonant stems take -을수록 (먹을수록, 작을수록) and vowel stems take -ㄹ수록 (갈수록, 클수록), while ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ first (살수록). A natural example is 한국어는 공부할수록 재미있어요 (the more you study Korean, the more fun it becomes), and Koreans love to double it up with -(으)면, as in 보면 볼수록 (the more you look, the more...). Two pitfalls: do not use -을수록 after a vowel, so it is 갈수록 not 갈을수록; and write 수록 right onto the verb, never spaced as 할 수록. Adding 더 (more) in the second clause makes the rising effect even clearer.

title: In order to
plainEnglish: It states the purpose or goal you are doing the main action for.
whenToUse: Use -기 위해(서) to state a deliberate goal you are working toward, especially planned, intentional ones: 살을 빼기 위해서 매일 운동해요 (I exercise every day in order to lose weight). The intent is to spotlight the purpose behind your effort, so it suits goals like saving money, getting a job, or passing a test. It is slightly formal and very common in writing, presentations, and earnest spoken explanations. For a noun goal you switch to N을/를 위해서 (가족을 위해서 = for my family). The 위 here is the Sino-Korean 爲 meaning for the sake of, which is why both an action (기 위해서) and a noun (을/를 위해서) can plug into the same frame.
attachmentRule: Attach -기 위해서 (or the slightly more formal -기 위하여) to the plain verb stem with no change (빼다→빼기 위해서, 사다→사기 위해서). 위해 and 위해서 are interchangeable. For a noun goal, use N을/를 위해서 instead (가족을 위해서 = for my family). The subject usually intends the goal on purpose.
contrastWith: -기 위해서 vs -(으)러: both mean in order to, but -(으)러 attaches only to a purpose paired with motion verbs 가다/오다 (밥 먹으러 식당에 가요 = I go to the restaurant to eat), while -기 위해서 works with almost any main verb and is not limited to going and coming (밥을 먹기 위해서 요리해요). -기 위해서 vs -도록: 위해서 states a deliberate purpose you aim at, whereas -도록 sets a standard or result to keep, often preventing something (감기에 걸리지 않도록 조심해요).

examples.ko: 건강을 위해서 담배를 끊었어요.
examples.en: I quit smoking for the sake of my health.

examples.ko: 돈을 모으기 위해서 외식을 많이 줄였어요.
examples.en: I cut back on eating out a lot in order to save money.

examples.ko: 한국 회사에 취직하기 위해서 매일 한국어를 공부하고 있어요.
examples.en: I am studying Korean every day in order to get a job at a Korean company.

commonMistakes: Conjugating the verb before -기 위해서, like 빼서 위해서 or 빼고 위해서; use the plain stem plus -기, so 빼기 위해서, because 위해서 always follows the noun-like -기 form.
Using -기 위해서 with a noun, like 가족기 위해서; for nouns drop -기 and use N을/를 위해서, as in 가족을 위해서, since a noun cannot take the verb ending -기.

practiceItems.prompt: in order to lose weight (I exercise every day)
in order to save money (I cut back on eating out)
for the sake of my health (I quit smoking)

studyOrder: Decide the goal or purpose you are aiming for
If it is an action, add -기 위해서 to that verb stem
If it is a noun, use N을/를 위해서 instead
Put the action you take toward that goal in the main clause
beginnerExplanation: V-기 위해(서) is the clear, slightly formal way to state the purpose behind what you do, matching English in order to. The 위 comes from the Sino-Korean 爲 (for the sake of), a handy anchor for remembering its meaning. For an action goal you add -기 위해서 to the plain stem, so 빼다 becomes 빼기 위해서 in 살을 빼기 위해서 운동해요 (I exercise in order to lose weight); 위해 and 위해서 mean the same thing. When the goal is a noun, you switch to N을/를 위해서, as in 가족을 위해서 (for my family), so do not jam 기 onto a noun. The most common slip is conjugating the verb first, like 빼서 위해서; always keep the bare stem plus 기. Compare it with -(으)러, which also means in order to but only pairs with going and coming verbs, while 기 위해서 works with nearly any main verb and stresses a deliberate goal.

title: Because / and then
plainEnglish: It links a cause to its result, or one action to the next closely connected one.
whenToUse: Use -아/어서 to give a reason (늦어서 택시를 탔어요 = I was late, so I took a taxi) or to chain one action smoothly into a closely connected next one done by the same person (친구를 만나서 같이 커피를 마셨어요 = I met my friend and we had coffee). The intent is a tight, natural cause-result or sequence where the two halves genuinely depend on each other — the meeting is what made the coffee possible. It is the default, everyday because for explaining feelings, weather effects, and reactions: 배가 고파서, 피곤해서, 비가 와서. The crucial habit is that the first clause carries no tense and cannot be followed by a command or suggestion.
attachmentRule: Build the 아/어 connective by vowel harmony: if the last stem vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ use -아서 (가다→가서, 좋다→좋아서), otherwise use -어서 (먹다→먹어서, 늦다→늦어서); 하다 becomes 해서. Crucially, the first clause never takes a tense marker, so you say 늦어서, never 늦었어서, and you cannot use a command or suggestion after a reason -아/어서.
contrastWith: -아/어서 vs -(으)니까: -아/어서 gives a tight cause-result, stays tenseless, and cannot lead to a command or suggestion (피곤해서 쉬세요 is wrong). -(으)니까 is a because that DOES allow commands and suggestions (피곤하니까 쉬세요 = since you're tired, rest) and can carry tense in the first clause. So whenever the second clause is an order, a request, or a let's, you must use -(으)니까, not -아/어서. For pure feeling-reasons (좋아서, 무서워서), -아/어서 is the only natural choice.

examples.ko: 배가 고파서 라면을 끓였어요.
examples.en: I was hungry, so I made ramyeon.

examples.ko: 길이 미끄러워서 아주 조심히 걸었어요.
examples.en: The road was slippery, so I walked very carefully.

examples.ko: 감기에 걸려서 어제 회사를 못 갔어요.
examples.en: I caught a cold, so I could not go to work yesterday.

commonMistakes: Putting tense on the first clause, like 늦었어서 or 좋았어서; keep it tenseless as 늦어서 / 좋아서 and mark past or future only on the final verb, because 아/어서 itself never carries tense.
Using a command or suggestion after a reason -아/어서, like 피곤해서 쉬세요 or 시간이 없어서 빨리 가자; for those switch to -(으)니까 (피곤하니까 쉬세요), since -아/어서 cannot lead to an order or a let's.

practiceItems.prompt: I was hungry, so (I made ramyeon)
the road was slippery, so (I walked carefully)
I caught a cold, so (I could not go to work)

studyOrder: Find the cause or the first action
Make the 아/어 connective using vowel harmony
Keep that first clause tenseless
Add the result or next action, marking tense only at the end
beginnerExplanation: V/A-아/어서 is one of the most useful connectors in Korean, covering both because and a smooth and then between two tightly linked actions. You form it with the same vowel harmony as the present tense: ㅏ or ㅗ stems take -아서 (가서, 좋아서), other stems take -어서 (먹어서, 늦어서), and 하다 becomes 해서. So 배가 고파서 라면을 끓였어요 means I was hungry, so I made ramyeon. Two rules are essential, and a small chant helps: 아/어서 stays tenseless and never commands. First, mark past or future only on the final verb, so it is 늦어서, never 늦었어서. Second, you cannot follow a reason 아/어서 with a command or suggestion, so to tell someone to rest because they are tired you must switch to 피곤하니까 쉬세요 using 으니까 instead.

title: As soon as
plainEnglish: It says the second action happens immediately after the first one finishes.
whenToUse: Use -자마자 when one action ends and the next follows instantly, with essentially no gap: 집에 오자마자 침대에 누웠어요 (As soon as I got home, I lay down on the bed). The intent is to stress immediacy — the second the first thing was done, the next happened. It fits triggers and reflexes: 알람이 울리자마자 일어났어요, 월급을 받자마자 다 썼어요. Because the timing is so tight, Koreans often add 바로 (right away) for extra punch. If there is a normal pause or a sense of completing-then-doing-something-later, this is the wrong tool — that is -고 나서 territory.
attachmentRule: Attach -자마자 straight to the plain verb stem with no vowel change and regardless of consonant or vowel ending (오다→오자마자, 끝나다→끝나자마자, 받다→받자마자). It goes only on action verbs. The first clause carries no tense marker; the tense is shown on the final verb.
contrastWith: -자마자 vs -고 나서: -자마자 stresses an immediate, back-to-back sequence with almost no gap (집에 오자마자 잤어요 = the instant I got home, I slept), while -고 나서 means after finishing and allows a normal gap of time (집에 오고 나서 잤어요 = I got home and later slept). -자마자 vs -다가: -다가 leaves the first action unfinished and switches mid-way, whereas -자마자 requires the first action to be fully over before the second instantly begins.

examples.ko: 집에 오자마자 손을 씻었어요.
examples.en: As soon as I got home, I washed my hands.

examples.ko: 알람이 울리자마자 바로 일어났어요.
examples.en: As soon as the alarm rang, I got up right away.

examples.ko: 월급을 받자마자 카드값으로 다 나갔어요.
examples.en: As soon as I got my paycheck, it all went to the credit card bill.

commonMistakes: Putting tense on the first clause, like 왔자마자 or 받았자마자; attach -자마자 to the plain stem (오자마자, 받자마자) and show tense only on the final verb.
Using it for two actions with a long gap between them, like 졸업하자마자 십 년 후에 취직했어요; for a non-immediate after, use -고 나서 (졸업하고 나서 취직했어요) instead, since 자마자 demands near-instant follow-up.

practiceItems.prompt: as soon as I got home (I washed my hands)
as soon as the alarm rang (I got up)
as soon as class ended (I went straight home)

studyOrder: Find the first action that triggers the next
Attach -자마자 to its plain stem
Keep the first clause tenseless
Put the immediate next action in the second clause, often with 바로
beginnerExplanation: V-자마자 expresses that the moment one action finishes, the next one happens, just like English as soon as — imagine the two actions touching back-to-back with no space between them. It is wonderfully simple to attach: add -자마자 to the plain verb stem with no changes for vowels or consonants, so 오다 becomes 오자마자 and 받다 becomes 받자마자. A natural example is 집에 오자마자 침대에 누웠어요 (the second I got home, I flopped onto the bed). Keep the first clause tenseless and mark tense only at the end, so write 오자마자, not 왔자마자. The nuance is immediacy with essentially no gap, which is why you often add 바로 (right away); when there is a normal pause between the two actions, use -고 나서 instead to mean simply after finishing.

title: So that / until
plainEnglish: It sets a goal or limit that the main action aims toward, often so that something happens.
whenToUse: Use -도록 to set a result, standard, or limit that your main action works toward, very often in advice and instructions: 감기에 걸리지 않도록 옷을 따뜻하게 입어요 (I dress warmly so that I don't catch a cold). The intent is to aim at an outcome to achieve or, frequently, to prevent (지 않도록). It is the natural ending for guidance and rules: 잘 듣도록 크게 말해 주세요, 잊어버리지 않도록 메모하세요. It also marks a time limit meaning up to a point: 밤늦도록 일했어요 (I worked until late at night). So -도록 spans two senses, a target-result and an until-boundary, and context tells them apart.
attachmentRule: Attach -도록 to the plain verb stem with no vowel change (늦다→늦도록, 알다→알도록, 들리다→들리도록). It commonly appears in the negative as -지 않도록 (so that ... not) and in advice or instructions. It can also mean until a point, as in 밤늦도록 (until late at night).
contrastWith: -도록 vs -기 위해서: -기 위해서 names a deliberate purpose you intend (취직하기 위해서 공부해요 = I study in order to get a job), while -도록 sets a result or standard to keep, and it especially shines for preventing things (감기에 걸리지 않도록 = so that you don't catch a cold), where 위해서 sounds awkward. -도록 vs -게: both can mean so that; -게 is lighter and very common in speech (잘 보이게 = so it's visible), while -도록 feels a touch more formal and directive, common in written instructions.

examples.ko: 다른 사람들이 잘 듣도록 크게 말해 주세요.
examples.en: Please speak loudly so that others can hear well.

examples.ko: 잊어버리지 않도록 휴대폰에 메모를 해 뒀어요.
examples.en: I made a note on my phone so that I would not forget.

examples.ko: 어제는 밤늦도록 일하느라 잠을 거의 못 잤어요.
examples.en: Yesterday I worked until late at night, so I barely slept.

commonMistakes: Adding vowel harmony before -도록, like 듣어도록 or 알아도록; attach it to the plain stem, so 듣도록 and 알도록, with no -아/어 inserted.

Forgetting the natural negative shape -지 않도록 for so that ... not, like saying 안 늦도록 instead of 늦지 않도록; the smooth, idiomatic form for preventing something is always -지 않도록 (늦지 않도록 = so as not to be late).

practiceItems.prompt: so that others can hear well (please speak loudly)
practiceItems.ko: 다른 사람들이 잘 듣도록 크게 말해 주세요.
practiceItems.answer: 다른 사람들이 잘 듣도록 크게 말해 주세요.

practiceItems.prompt: so that you do not catch a cold (dress warmly)
practiceItems.ko: 감기에 걸리지 않도록 옷을 따뜻하게 입으세요.
practiceItems.answer: 감기에 걸리지 않도록 옷을 따뜻하게 입으세요.

practiceItems.prompt: so that I would not forget (I made a note)

studyOrder: Decide the result or limit you are aiming for
Attach -도록 to the verb stem
Use -지 않도록 when the goal is to prevent something
Put the action that works toward it in the main clause
beginnerExplanation: V-도록 marks the goal, standard, or limit that your main action is reaching toward, and it is everywhere in advice and instructions — think of it as pointing an arrow at the outcome you want. You attach -도록 to the plain verb stem, so 듣다 becomes 듣도록 and 늦다 becomes 늦도록. Often the aim is to prevent something, which shows up as the negative -지 않도록: 감기에 걸리지 않도록 옷을 따뜻하게 입어요 means I dress warmly so that I do not catch a cold. It can also mark a time limit meaning until, as in 밤늦도록 일했어요 (I worked until late at night). Two tips: attach it to the bare stem, not a harmonized form like 듣어도록; and for so that not, prefer the smooth 지 않도록 over patching 안 in front. It overlaps with 기 위해서 but leans toward a result or rule you want to keep.

title: Busy doing, so couldn't
plainEnglish: It gives a time- or effort-consuming action as the reason you could not do something else.
whenToUse: Use -느라(고) when you were tied up doing one action and that is exactly why something else failed or could not happen: 드라마를 보느라고 숙제를 못 했어요 (I was busy watching a drama, so I couldn't do my homework). The intent is an excuse or apology built around your own time-and-energy drain, so the second clause is typically negative — 못 받았어요, 시간이 없었어요, 한숨도 못 잤어요. The same person must do both halves, and it only attaches to action verbs because being busy implies activity. It often appears when explaining lateness, missed calls, or exhaustion: 일하느라, 아이를 돌보느라, 기다리느라.
attachmentRule: Attach -느라(고) to an action verb stem with no vowel change (보다→보느라고, 일하다→일하느라고, 자다→자느라고); -느라 and -느라고 are interchangeable. The same person must do both actions, it goes only on action verbs, and the second clause is normally negative or apologetic. Do not add a tense marker before it.
contrastWith: -느라(고) vs -아/어서: -느라고 blames YOUR own time- or effort-consuming action for a negative result and demands the same subject (게임하느라고 전화를 못 받았어요 = I was busy gaming, so I missed the call), while -아/어서 is a neutral because that allows positive results and even different subjects (전화벨이 울려서 받았어요). -느라(고) vs -는 바람에: 느라고 is about your own absorbing activity, whereas 바람에 usually blames a sudden external event that hit you, and 바람에 does not require the same subject.

examples.ko: 게임하느라고 전화를 못 받았어요.
examples.en: I was busy gaming, so I missed your call.

examples.ko: 밤새 아이를 돌보느라고 한숨도 못 잤어요.
examples.en: I was busy looking after the kid all night, so I could not sleep a wink.

examples.ko: 퇴근 시간에 버스를 기다리느라고 약속에 한참 늦었어요.
examples.en: I was busy waiting for the bus at rush hour, so I was quite late to my appointment.

commonMistakes: Using it with an adjective or with two different subjects, like 바쁘느라고 or 제가 일하느라고 동생이 잤어요; it needs the same person doing an action verb, so an adjective reason should use -아/어서 (바빠서) and a different doer needs a separate clause.
Pairing it with a positive, happy result, like 영화를 보느라고 행복했어요; the second clause should be a negative or unable outcome (often with 못 or 안), so for a pleasant result switch to -아/어서 (영화를 봐서 행복했어요).

practiceItems.prompt: I was busy gaming, so (I missed your call)
I was busy with my part-time job, so (I had no time to study)
I was busy waiting for the bus, so (I was late)

studyOrder: Find the action that ate up your time or energy
Attach -느라(고) to that action verb stem
Make sure the same person does both actions
State the negative result, often with 못 or 안, in the second clause
beginnerExplanation: V-느라(고) explains that you were tied up doing one thing, and that is why something else did not get done — think of it as my time got swallowed by this, so that fell through. You attach -느라고 (or just -느라) to an action verb stem, so 보다 becomes 보느라고 and 일하다 becomes 일하느라고. The feel is always an excuse for a negative outcome with one subject: 드라마를 보느라고 숙제를 못 했어요 means I was busy watching a drama, so I could not do my homework. Three things keep it correct: it attaches only to action verbs, both actions must be done by the same person, and the result clause should be negative or apologetic, frequently with 못 or 안. That negative-result requirement is what separates it from the all-purpose 아/어서, which happily allows good results and different subjects.

title: After finishing
plainEnglish: It says you completely finish one action before starting the next.
whenToUse: Use -고 나서 to stress that the first action is fully done and only then do you move to the next: 손을 씻고 나서 밥을 먹어요 (I wash my hands and then eat). The intent is to highlight completion as a clear step — first this is finished, then that begins, with a normal amount of time allowed in between. It fits routines and sequences where order and finishing matter: 운동하고 나서 샤워했어요, 숙제를 다 하고 나서 게임했어요. Because it implies completion, it only works with action verbs. The 나다 inside it adds the nuance of having come out the other side of an action, reinforcing the done feeling.
attachmentRule: Attach -고 나서 to the plain verb stem with no vowel change for both vowel and consonant endings (먹다→먹고 나서, 씻다→씻고 나서, 하다→하고 나서). It goes on action verbs only, since it implies completion. The tense is marked on the final verb, not on the -고 나서 clause.
contrastWith: -고 나서 vs plain -고: plain -고 just lists or sequences actions without stressing completion (밥을 먹고 갔어요 = I ate and went), while -고 나서 emphasizes that the first action is fully finished first (밥을 먹고 나서 갔어요 = after finishing eating, I went). -고 나서 vs -자마자: -자마자 means the next action follows instantly with no gap (오자마자 잤어요), whereas -고 나서 allows a normal pause. -고 나서 vs -다가: -다가 leaves the first action unfinished, the exact opposite of the completion that 고 나서 demands.

examples.ko: 운동하고 나서 샤워를 했어요.
examples.en: I worked out and then took a shower.

examples.ko: 밥을 다 먹고 나서 약을 먹어야 해요.
examples.en: I have to take the medicine after I finish eating.

examples.ko: 이 영화를 보고 나서 원작 책도 꼭 읽어 보고 싶어요.
examples.en: After watching this movie, I really want to read the original book too.

commonMistakes: Using -고 나서 with an adjective, like 예쁘고 나서; it needs an action verb because it implies finishing an action, and a state like 예쁘다 cannot be completed.
Adding tense before it, like 먹었고 나서 or 했고 나서; attach -고 나서 to the plain stem (먹고 나서) and mark tense only on the final verb, since the -고 나서 clause itself stays tenseless.

practiceItems.prompt: I worked out and then (took a shower)
after eating (I have to take medicine)
practiceItems.ko: 밥을 먹고 나서 약을 먹어야 해요.
practiceItems.answer: 밥을 먹고 나서 약을 먹어야 해요.

practiceItems.prompt: I finished all my homework and then (played games)
practiceItems.ko: 숙제를 다 하고 나서 게임을 했어요.
practiceItems.answer: 숙제를 다 하고 나서 게임을 했어요.

studyOrder: Find the action you fully complete first
Attach -고 나서 to its plain stem
Keep that clause tenseless
Put the next action in the second clause, marking tense at the end
beginnerExplanation: V-고 나서 tells the listener that you completely finish one action and only then start the next, putting a clear emphasis on completion — picture checking a box done before turning to the next task. You attach -고 나서 to the plain verb stem with no changes, so 먹다 becomes 먹고 나서 and 씻다 becomes 씻고 나서, as in 손을 씻고 나서 밥을 먹어요 (I wash my hands and then eat). Because it implies finishing, it only works with action verbs, and you mark tense on the final verb, never as 먹었고 나서. It is worth comparing three similar tools: plain -고 simply lists actions in order, -고 나서 stresses that the first one is done, and -다가 means you broke off the first action partway to do the second. When the finish really matters, 고 나서 is the natural choice.
